title: Defects in the works of the godly are accidental; in the graceless, essential
source_text: XX. Verum est quidem etiam piorum & justorum opera per gratiam Dei facta suos quoque naevos & defectus habere; sed hi defectus sunt tantum accidentales, qui boni operis essentiam non tollunt. Qui vero vitiant opera eorum qui sunt Christi gratia destituti, sunt defectus essentiales, cum quibus salva manere non potest ipsa boni operis natura atque essentia. Siquidem operis bonitas praecipue pendet a fine in quem tendit, & a principio unde oritur. Sed hominis qui est gratiae Christi expers, opera omnia, ut supra ostendimus, & a vero fine aberrant, qui est Dei gloria; & a malo principio, cupiditate, scilicet, terrena originem ducunt: per quae opus alioqui ex suo genere bonum, omnino vitiatur. Piorum vero & justorum opera procedunt a Dei amore, & ad ejus gloriam tendunt, ac in eo solum deficiunt, quod nec in iis tam pure Dei gloria quaeritur, nec Dei amor unde fluunt tantum fervorem habet, quam par esset. Adeoque piorum opera imperfecte quidem sed vere bona sunt; eorum vero qui gratia Christi carent opera quaevis, ut ut in oculis hominum luceant, coram Deo revera mala sunt, nec boni operis naturam retinent: licet alia sint aliis minus mala.
pass_a_gloss: XX. True it is indeed that even the works of the pious and just done through the grace of God have also their blemishes and defects; but these defects are only accidental, which do not take away the essence of a good work. But those which vitiate the works of those who are destitute of the grace of Christ, are essential defects, with which the very nature and essence of a good work cannot remain safe. Since the goodness of a work chiefly depends on the end to which it tends, and on the principle whence it arises. But of the man who is without the grace of Christ, the works all, as we showed above, both from the true end stray, which is God's glory; and from a bad principle, namely earthly cupidity, take their origin: through which a work otherwise by its kind good, is altogether vitiated. But the works of the pious and just proceed from the love of God, and to his glory tend, and in this only fall short, that neither in them so purely is God's glory sought, nor has the love of God whence they flow so much fervour, as were fitting. And so the works of the pious imperfectly indeed but truly are good; but of those who lack the grace of Christ any works, however much in the eyes of men they shine, before God are in truth bad, nor retain the nature of a good work: although some be less bad than others.
pass_b_english: Thesis XX. It is true that even the works of the godly and righteous, done through God's grace, have their own blemishes and defects. But those defects are only accidental and do not take away the essence of a good work. The defects that spoil the works of those without the grace of Christ are essential ones, and the very nature and essence of a good work cannot survive them. A work's goodness depends chiefly on the end it tends to and the principle it springs from.

Yet all the works of a man without the grace of Christ, as shown above, miss the true end, which is God's glory, and take their origin from a bad principle, earthly desire. That ruins a work that would otherwise be good in its kind. The works of the godly and righteous proceed from love of God and tend to his glory. Their only shortfall is that God's glory is not sought in them as purely as it should be, and the love of God they flow from is not as fervent as it ought to be.

So the works of the godly are good, imperfectly but truly. Whatever works are done by those who lack the grace of Christ, however brightly they shine in men's eyes, are really bad before God and do not keep the nature of a good work, though some are less bad than others.
